lessons.title: Your first five minutes
lessons.prerequisites: Genesis installed on your Windows computer. Internet for the first model download or cloud setup.

steps.title: Give Genesis a brain

anchor.label: More options (cloud key, choose a model myself)

steps.narrationDraft: Genesis is the app you use. A model is the part that works out an answer, a little like choosing an engine for a car. You need one connected model before you can talk. On the welcome screen, choose automatic local setup, or open More options to choose a cloud service or local model yourself.
steps.checkpoint: You can see the welcome screen and a setup choice.
steps.tip: Local means the model runs on your computer. Cloud means a company’s computers answer over the internet.

steps.title: Choose the setup that suits you
steps.narrationDraft: Automatic setup offers a model sized for your computer and downloads what it needs. Leave Genesis open while the download finishes. If you already use a cloud service, open the cloud setup, enter that service’s API key and model, and use its connection test. A key is a private password for a service; a model name is the exact name of the brain you chose.
steps.checkpoint: Setup reports success before you move on.
steps.tip: A saved model name alone does not download a local model. Automatic setup is the easiest route when you are starting fresh.

steps.title: You can finish extras later
steps.narrationDraft: Once setup finishes, you reach the conversation. Settings → Finish setting up offers better speech recognition, browser setup and the phone connection. Each is optional. You can skip an extra and return to it later from Settings or Help.
steps.checkpoint: You know where to return for optional setup.

steps.title: Try something small
steps.narrationDraft: Click Conversation in the left panel. Click the message box and type: “Help me plan three easy dinners. Ask me what food I have first.” Press Enter, or the round arrow button. Use Shift+Enter when you want a new line without sending.
steps.checkpoint: Your question appears in the conversation and Genesis answers.
steps.tip: Tell it what you want in ordinary words. You do not need special commands.

steps.title: Make the answer useful to you
steps.narrationDraft: Answer its question, or ask: “Make that simpler” or “Put it in a shopping list.” Genesis can help with writing, explanations, files, research and tasks. Connected tools make more actions available. Read results before relying on them, and tell it when something is wrong.
steps.checkpoint: You have a useful answer and know how to ask for a change.

lessons.title: Find your way around
lessons.prerequisites: An open Genesis window.

steps.title: Start with the left panel
steps.narrationDraft: The left panel is your map. Conversation is everyday chat. Projects holds work on a board. Schedule holds timed tasks. Missions handles a bigger objective. Lower down are Memory, Plugins, Activity, System Feed, Settings and Discoveries. If the panel is hidden, click the three-line Navigation icon at the top.
steps.checkpoint: You can open the navigation and find Settings.

steps.title: The middle is your work area

anchor.label: Choose primary model from saved templates

steps.narrationDraft: Your selected page appears in the middle. In Conversation, replies appear above the message box. The paperclip attaches a file, the microphone dictates text, and the arrow sends it. The model name opens your saved model chooser. Small arrows open extra choices; hovering over an icon reveals its name.
steps.checkpoint: You can identify the attachment, microphone, send and model controls.

steps.title: Open the activity panel
steps.narrationDraft: Click the panel icon at the upper right. Activity & context shows the current tool, context usage and memory totals. Context is the amount of material the model can hold in a single request. This panel is different from the Activity page in the left navigation, which shows usage over time.
steps.checkpoint: You can open and close the right-hand panel.

steps.title: Use the menus at the top
steps.narrationDraft: File starts a new conversation and opens Settings. Edit has copy, paste and other text actions. View changes the interface, theme, text style and browser view. Help opens the built-in guide and setup extras. Menu items with a small arrow or a chooser reveal more options.
steps.checkpoint: You know where to change the look and where to get help.

steps.title: Modern and Classic share the same work
steps.narrationDraft: The Classic / Modern switch changes the arrangement. Classic shows labelled mode buttons and more controls at once. Modern uses more compact icons and menus. View → Toggle light / dark theme changes the colours. Your conversations and settings belong to the same Genesis, whichever view you choose.
steps.checkpoint: You can switch layouts and return to the one you prefer.
steps.tip: The screenshots here use the current development interface. An older installed release may place a control differently.

lessons.title: Chat, follow up and start fresh
lessons.prerequisites: A connected model.

steps.title: Say what the finished result should be
steps.narrationDraft: Try: “Write a friendly birthday invitation. Keep it short. Ask me for the date and place.” Include the goal, helpful facts and any limits. If you want ideas only, say so. If you want it to create a file, say which folder and file you want.
steps.checkpoint: Your message clearly names the result you want.

steps.title: Read the answer and the tool rows
steps.narrationDraft: Genesis may answer directly or use tools to read, search or create something. Tool rows in the conversation can be expanded to see the arguments and result. A tool is one action, such as reading a file. An answer saying something is done should agree with the resulting file or page.
steps.checkpoint: You know to open a tool row when you want to understand an action.

steps.title: Send a follow-up while it works

anchor.label: Send during response (Enter with empty composer)

steps.narrationDraft: In Modern, a message sent during work normally waits After response. Its waiting card appears above the message box. Send now offers a text-only message at the next work step; you can also press Enter with an empty message box to promote the most recent eligible message. Attachments wait until after the reply. In Classic, the Queue selector offers the delivery choices.
steps.checkpoint: You can recognise a waiting message and choose whether to send its text during work.
steps.tip: Sending now can steer a running task; it does not undo an action already taken. Pause or stop first when no further action should happen before your correction.

steps.title: Inspect the waiting messages
steps.narrationDraft: Open Queue from the conversation view chooser below the Modern message box, or its labelled tab in Classic. Each message can be edited, moved up or down, or removed. Clear all removes all waiting messages. Read what is waiting before a long task continues.
steps.checkpoint: Only the messages you still want remain in the queue.

steps.title: Start a new conversation
steps.narrationDraft: Use File → New conversation for a new subject. Open Saved conversations to return to an older one. A new conversation clears the visible thread for a fresh start; it does not erase Genesis’s long-term memory.
steps.checkpoint: You can start a fresh thread and find an older one.

lessons.title: Share files, pictures and screenshots
lessons.prerequisites: A small file or image you are comfortable sharing with your chosen model.

steps.title: Choose the file
steps.narrationDraft: Click the paperclip beside the message box, or drag a file onto the conversation. Documents, images and code give Genesis material to work with. A ZIP can hold a whole project. Keep the first example small: a short document is easier to follow than a large folder.
steps.checkpoint: The file appears beside your draft before you send it.

steps.title: Tell Genesis what to do with it
steps.narrationDraft: An attachment alone does not explain your goal. Write “Summarise this in five simple points,” “Find the date in this letter,” or “Explain this error message.” Check that the right file is attached. Here, garden-notes.txt is waiting beside the draft. Remove a mistaken attachment before you send.
steps.checkpoint: The draft contains both the right file and a clear instruction.

steps.title: Press Send when you are ready
steps.narrationDraft: Press the arrow or Enter. The file is now part of your request. Open Attachments in the conversation view chooser to inspect attached items later. Images need a model or secondary vision helper that can read pictures; the Vision lesson explains that setup.
steps.checkpoint: The sent message shows the attachment and Genesis starts working.
steps.tip: If your model is in the cloud, relevant content can be sent to that service. Choose a local model for material you want processed locally.

steps.title: Find and check generated files
steps.narrationDraft: If you ask Genesis to create a document or code, ask it to say where it saved the result. Open the file and check it. For code work, Settings → Code offers history, safe copies and review. A preview in the conversation is useful, but the finished file is what you should inspect.
steps.checkpoint: You can locate the resulting file on your computer.

lessons.title: Settings, one room at a time
lessons.prerequisites: Settings open from the left panel or File menu.

steps.title: Pick the right section
steps.narrationDraft: Models chooses the brain. Voice & Vision chooses listening, speech and images. Computer use controls what Genesis may operate and includes Appshots and pets. Plugins holds tools, connections, MCP servers and hooks.
steps.checkpoint: You can find the section for the change you want.

steps.title: The other sections
steps.narrationDraft: Communications connects Telegram and your phone. Code holds code folders, history, safe copies, reviews and GitHub. Missions holds bigger-job settings and role models. Memory holds memory options, health and backups. System holds general behaviour, tools and display choices.
steps.checkpoint: You can tell which section owns a setting.

steps.title: Look for Save changes
steps.narrationDraft: Most model and voice edits stay in the form until you click Save changes. Some controls, including Computer use and desktop extras, say they apply immediately. Follow the note next to the control. A switch that looks on in an unsaved form is not proof the running app has adopted it.
steps.checkpoint: You see a saved confirmation after a change that needs saving.

steps.title: Change one thing, then try it
steps.narrationDraft: Make one change at a time and try a small task. If something stops working, you know which change to revisit. For unfamiliar numbers, leave the recommended or default setting and open the matching lesson first.
steps.checkpoint: You have a simple way to check each change.

lessons.title: Make the window comfortable to read
lessons.prerequisites: An open Genesis window.

steps.title: Choose your layout
steps.narrationDraft: Open View, or use Classic / Modern. Classic gives you more labelled controls at once. Modern leaves more space for the conversation. Try both with the same conversation and choose the one you find easier.
steps.checkpoint: The layout feels comfortable to use.

steps.title: Choose the colours and text style
steps.narrationDraft: View → Toggle light / dark theme changes the colour theme. The Genesis text / Compact text choice changes message typography. This is a reading preference, separate from the model’s writing style. Ask Genesis to write more simply if the words themselves are too difficult.
steps.checkpoint: You can comfortably read the messages.

steps.title: Show timestamps when you want them
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → System → Chat display. Show message times in Chat adds a time beneath chat messages. Activity and memory logs already have times. This display preference takes effect in the interface.
steps.checkpoint: You can tell when a message was sent.

steps.title: Choose how code changes appear
steps.narrationDraft: Expand code changes by default opens change details automatically. Leave it off if you prefer a compact chat and open individual changes yourself. This changes the presentation; it does not approve, test or apply the code.
steps.checkpoint: Code details open only as often as you prefer.

lessons.title: Connect a model on your computer
lessons.prerequisites: A downloaded local model, or the first-run automatic setup. Enough disk space and memory for that model.

steps.title: Understand the two local routes
steps.narrationDraft: Ollama manages downloaded models by name. llama.cpp loads a model file, usually ending in .gguf. Both can run the brain on your computer. Downloading a model initially needs internet; after setup, local inference can work offline. Internet tools still need internet.
steps.checkpoint: You have chosen Ollama or llama.cpp.

steps.title: Open Models and create a template
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Models → New. Give the template an easy name such as “My everyday local model.” A template, also called a preset, is a saved model connection and its settings. Choosing a preset later saves you from typing the connection again.
steps.checkpoint: The New template window is open.

steps.title: For Ollama, match the model name
steps.narrationDraft: Choose Ollama (local). Keep the local endpoint if Ollama is on this computer. Enter the exact installed model name. The example qwen3:8b only works when that model is installed in Ollama. Genesis’s automatic welcome setup can download a model for you; typing a name in Models does not download it.
steps.checkpoint: The model name matches an installed Ollama model.
steps.tip: An endpoint is the address of the model service. “127.0.0.1” means this computer.

steps.title: For llama.cpp, choose your GGUF file
steps.narrationDraft: Choose llama.cpp (local). Enter the GGUF model path and check the endpoint. Genesis can load a configured local model when selected. If you already run your own server, use its address and matching model setup. GPU layers controls how much work goes to the graphics card; start with the supplied settings.
steps.checkpoint: The file path points to an existing GGUF model.

steps.title: Save a modest starting configuration
steps.narrationDraft: Leave the model’s recommended generation settings in place. Large context sizes and large models need more memory. A context number in Genesis does not give a model more capacity than its server or hardware supports. Save the template, choose it, and press Save changes in the Models page.
steps.checkpoint: The selected primary is the local model you configured.

steps.title: Say hello and check the answer

anchor.label: Choose primary model from saved templates

steps.narrationDraft: Return to Conversation and send a short hello. If it cannot connect, check that the local model service is running, the address is right and the name matches. If it is very slow or runs out of memory, try a smaller model or smaller supported context.
steps.checkpoint: A real answer arrives from your local model.

lessons.title: Connect a cloud model
lessons.prerequisites: An account and API key from the provider you chose. Internet access.

steps.title: Choose where answers will come from
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Models. The provider choices include NVIDIA Cloud, Nebius Token Factory, Anthropic, and Custom (OpenAI-compatible). Custom is for a service that accepts the compatible API format. A chat website subscription and an API account may be separate; use the key for the service’s API.
steps.checkpoint: You have selected the provider you actually have access to.

steps.title: Keep the connection details together
steps.narrationDraft: Choose a matching preset or make a new template. For providers with an Endpoint URL, use the base address supplied by that provider. Enter the exact Model name available to your API account. Example names and example URLs are placeholders, not a working account.
steps.checkpoint: Provider, endpoint and model name all belong to the same service.

steps.title: Enter your key in its own field
steps.narrationDraft: Paste the provider’s API key into the key field on the Models page. Keys are stored separately from templates. Do not put your real key in a screenshot or shared example. Parse code does not fill the key field; a copied example is not a substitute for entering the key here.
steps.checkpoint: The provider key field reports that a key is set after saving.

steps.title: Use the provider’s supported settings
steps.narrationDraft: Start with a supplied preset or the provider’s example connection code. Some providers do not accept every generation control. A disabled parameter switch leaves that form parameter out where supported. Provider-specific thinking profiles belong to the matching model, not every model you own.
steps.checkpoint: Your settings match what the provider supports.

steps.title: Save and try a short request

anchor.label: Choose primary model from saved templates

steps.narrationDraft: Click Save changes, return to Conversation and send a short request. A wrong model name, expired key, exhausted quota or incorrect address can prevent a reply. Check those first. The Backup lesson shows how a second model can help when the primary becomes unavailable.
steps.checkpoint: You receive an answer before trying a larger task.
steps.tip: Cloud usage may have charges or limits set by the provider. Genesis’s activity totals are not your provider’s bill.

lessons.title: Add a model by pasting connection code
lessons.prerequisites: A provider’s example Python, cURL, Node or compatible connection snippet. Use an example without your real secret.

steps.title: Start with the provider and key
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Models and choose the right provider, or use New for a separate template. Enter the actual API key in the provider’s key field. The parser reads the example as text; it does not run the pasted program, install a model or create a provider account.
steps.checkpoint: You are editing the intended provider or template.

steps.title: Open the optional code panel
steps.narrationDraft: Find Paste connection code (optional) and click Show. Paste the provider’s connection example. It can contain the model name, base URL and request settings. The example in this tutorial uses a deliberately nonworking example address and key placeholder. For your model, copy the provider’s real documented values.
steps.checkpoint: The connection snippet is visible in the text box.

steps.title: Click Parse code and review the result
steps.narrationDraft: Click Parse code. Genesis extracts values it recognises, redacts key text in the saved snippet, and shows detected information or warnings. When it finds a model and base URL, those fill the relevant form fields. Image capability and thinking profiles can also be detected. Check the result; unusual code may not be fully understood.
steps.checkpoint: The imported checklist contains the values you expected.
steps.tip: Do not assume the parser chose a different provider for you. Check the provider yourself. It never reads the real API key into the key field.

steps.title: Understand which value will be sent
steps.narrationDraft: With Apply pasted parameters to this model on, each checked imported key wins over the matching form value. In our example, imported temperature = 0.7 wins even if the temperature field still displays 0.3. The field can be dimmed and labelled “Pasted code applies temperature.” The summary labels imported values “pasted.”
steps.checkpoint: You can identify the value that will actually control the next request.
steps.tip: Temperature affects how varied answers are. The pasted value is active; a visible old slider value is not necessarily the value being sent.

steps.title: Give one setting back to its slider
steps.narrationDraft: To control temperature from the normal form again, uncheck temperature in the imported checklist. Then enable and adjust the form’s Temperature control. Other checked imported keys still apply. To stop using all pasted parameters together, turn off the master Apply pasted parameters switch.
steps.checkpoint: Only the imported keys you want remain active.

steps.title: Know the separate settings
steps.narrationDraft: Imported max_tokens or max_completion_tokens can replace the form’s output limit. seed may have no normal slider. The Context window is Genesis’s prompt budget and local-server setting; it is not simply another pasted request parameter. Active thinking ON/OFF profiles can override pasted thinking-related settings when thinking changes.
steps.checkpoint: You know which settings are separate from the imported checklist.

steps.title: Save both the configuration and the template you need
steps.narrationDraft: Check the provider, URL, model name, key status and imported values. In an existing Models form, Save changes applies the edited configuration. Update template saves changes back into the selected reusable template. In a New template window, use Create template, then Save changes on the Models page. Test a short message.
steps.checkpoint: The chosen model answers with the saved configuration.

steps.title: Switch models without carrying the old example along
steps.narrationDraft: When you select a different saved preset, its own settings replace the model-specific pasted configuration. Old presets without imported values receive neutral defaults. Keep separate presets for different models. Clear removes the imported snippet and keys; review any separately detected thinking profiles or image capability afterward.
steps.checkpoint: Each preset has the connection and parameters intended for that model.

lessons.title: Understand model settings
lessons.prerequisites: Settings → Models open. Start with a working preset.

steps.title: Context is the model’s working desk
steps.narrationDraft: Context window is how much text can fit into one model request: instructions, conversation, memories and tools. Max output tokens limits one generated reply. A token is a small piece of text, not necessarily a whole word. More output leaves less room for input within the total window.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish the input workspace from the length of one answer.

steps.title: Use a size your model can really handle
steps.narrationDraft: Genesis checks model limits and local memory where possible. Trust my context window overrides some local safeguards; use it only when both the server and hardware support your chosen size. Context framing reserve keeps room for chat and tool formatting. Turning off the form’s context switch does not remove Genesis’s internal safe prompt budget.
steps.checkpoint: The context choice agrees with your model and server.

steps.title: Variety and repetition controls
steps.narrationDraft: Temperature adjusts variation. Top-P and Top-K adjust which possible next words can be considered. Presence penalty and Repeat penalty affect repetition when supported. These are optional fine-tuning controls. Keep the model’s recommended values until you have a specific problem to solve.
steps.checkpoint: You know what these controls broadly mean without needing to change them.

steps.title: Reasoning and streaming
steps.narrationDraft: The reasoning chooser appears according to the model’s abilities. Use profile follows the saved configuration; supported models may offer Off, Low, Medium or High. Stream mode shows words as they arrive; off waits for a full reply. Streaming changes presentation, not whether Genesis can use tools.
steps.checkpoint: You can choose a supported reasoning level and recognise streaming.

steps.title: Advanced profiles and mood-following thinking
steps.narrationDraft: Advanced thinking profiles and Custom reasoning levels describe provider-specific request settings. Use the provider’s supported values; invented level names do not give a model new abilities. Thinking follows mood, when enabled, adjusts effort within your selected ceiling for supported models. It does not add reasoning levels to a model that has none.
steps.checkpoint: You understand why some controls are unavailable for a particular model.

lessons.title: Keep going with a backup model
lessons.prerequisites: Two working saved model presets. A local backup can work when a cloud service is unavailable.

steps.title: Save the backup first
steps.narrationDraft: Connect and test your second model, then save it as a preset. A backup must be able to answer on its own. Selecting an uninstalled local model or a cloud model without a valid key will not provide a working backup.
steps.checkpoint: Both the primary and backup have answered a small test.

steps.title: Choose Backup model
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Models → Companion failover — not Missions. Choose the second preset under Backup model and click Save changes. This covers Chat, Work, Autonomy and companion helpers. The compact Backup chooser below the Modern message box also selects a saved backup.
steps.checkpoint: The backup status reports standby or current fallback use.

steps.title: Know what makes it switch

anchor.label: Using backup: Qwen3 8B (Ollama). Next request will retry primary.

steps.narrationDraft: If the primary fails before delivering an answer—for example because of a provider usage limit, rate limit, timeout or outage—Genesis can retry through the configured backup. It carries the working request forward. Content or tool work already delivered is not blindly replayed on the backup, so fallback is not a promise that every partial failure can be recovered.
steps.checkpoint: You recognise the backup status when the demonstration shows it.

steps.title: Your primary choice stays saved

anchor.label: Using backup: Qwen3 8B (Ollama). Next request will retry primary.

steps.narrationDraft: The primary’s saved connection remains your primary. The status explains which model is actually answering, separately from your chosen primary. Your backup might be less capable: a smaller local model may give a simpler answer, and it may need a separate vision helper for pictures.
steps.checkpoint: You can tell a configured primary from the effective backup.

steps.title: Return happens on a real request
steps.narrationDraft: Retry primary after (minutes) is the cooldown. After it passes, the next real request tests the primary. Success returns to primary; failure starts another waiting period. Genesis does not make a paid background ping just because the timer expires. A backend restart starts with the saved primary again.
steps.checkpoint: You understand why the status can say the next request will retry.

steps.title: Missions have a separate backup for each role
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Missions → Role models for mission primary and backup choices. The companion backup does not govern Missions. Each role may use a different model and has its own failover window for provider rate limits. Check these before a big job.
steps.checkpoint: You know where to set the mission’s independent model choices.
steps.tip: Usage limits are different from a full context window or a task’s step budget. A backup does not remove those other limits.

lessons.title: Use your voice instead of typing
lessons.prerequisites: A microphone. Enable voice features in Settings → Voice & Vision.

steps.title: Turn on voice features
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Voice & Vision and enable Enable voice features. Start with Whisper (local, free) for Speech-to-text and Piper (local neural, free) for Text-to-speech. Click Save changes. Listening and speaking are separate choices; they do not change your main AI model.
steps.checkpoint: Voice is enabled and the choices are saved.

steps.title: Dictate into the message box
steps.narrationDraft: Click the microphone beside the message box and speak clearly. Dictation turns speech into draft text. Stop recording using the microphone control, check the recognised words, edit any mistake, then press Send. This gives you a chance to correct names, numbers and dates before sending.
steps.checkpoint: Your spoken words appear as editable text in the draft.
steps.tip: The first use may take a moment while the local speech engine loads. Check the selected microphone and Windows permission if it cannot start.

steps.title: Choose conversation for an ongoing exchange
steps.narrationDraft: The Voice entry opens an ongoing spoken exchange rather than simply filling the draft. The circle beside it opens the minimal orb view. In conversation mode, spoken turns are sent as the conversation proceeds. Use the mute and exit controls when you want it to stop listening.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish draft dictation from an ongoing voice session.

steps.title: Listen to an existing reply
steps.narrationDraft: Use a reply’s read-aloud control when you want to hear text already on screen. Autonomous speech in Voice settings controls when Genesis may speak without a play click. Choose On request only if you want quiet unless you explicitly ask for speech.
steps.checkpoint: You have chosen when Genesis may speak.

lessons.title: Improve speech recognition
lessons.prerequisites: Settings → Voice & Vision. Internet for an optional download.

steps.title: Speech-to-text listens; it does not answer
steps.narrationDraft: Whisper turns audio into words. Your language model then answers those words. Changing Whisper changes recognition, not the brain’s knowledge or personality. The bundled base model gets you started. A larger recognition model can help with other languages and harder audio, at a memory and speed cost.
steps.checkpoint: You know which part is recognising your voice.

steps.title: Choose the languages you speak
steps.narrationDraft: Use Languages you speak → Add a language. Selecting your languages helps avoid a similar language being mistaken for yours. Leave the list empty only if you want recognition to consider any language. A single Whisper model supports multiple languages; you do not need a separate download for each language.
steps.checkpoint: The languages you actually use appear in the list.

steps.title: Pick a size and download it
steps.narrationDraft: Open Whisper model. Automatic chooses the recommended size for this computer once available. A missing size offers a Download button and shows its size. Click Download and wait for completion. Progress can resume after a dropped connection. Choose the size, then save changes.
steps.checkpoint: The selected model is installed, and you have checked “In use now.”

steps.title: Read In use now
steps.narrationDraft: The size you choose and the size currently running can differ. If a size is not downloaded or does not fit in free memory, Genesis uses an installed size that fits. In use now tells you which one is actually active. Freeing memory or choosing a smaller size can help on an older computer.
steps.checkpoint: You can explain why “Automatic small” might currently be using base.

steps.title: Leave the device on Automatic to start
steps.narrationDraft: Whisper device → Automatic uses the NVIDIA graphics card only when there is room and a local AI model is not competing for it. Otherwise recognition uses the processor. Selecting graphics-card recognition may require the optional NVIDIA libraries, offered with a download button. The processor remains a useful choice.
steps.checkpoint: The “Running on” line tells you the active device.

steps.title: Try a short sentence and compare
steps.narrationDraft: Dictate a short sentence with a name and a number. Correct any mistakes in the draft. If recognition is poor, reduce background noise, check your languages, and compare an installed larger size. Voice resources → Auto · save memory unloads idle engines; an active session is protected.
steps.checkpoint: Your next dictated sentence is understandable without a long wait.

lessons.title: Choose and download a speaking voice
lessons.prerequisites: Voice enabled. Internet only for a new voice download.

steps.title: Text-to-speech is the speaking part
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Voice & Vision → Text-to-speech. Piper is a local neural voice. Windows voices use installed system voices. Browser voices depend on the browser environment. The voice choice belongs to its selected engine; changing the engine changes the available voices.
steps.checkpoint: You have chosen the engine that will speak.

steps.title: Choose an installed voice
steps.narrationDraft: Open Voice and select an installed voice. The bundled Piper voice is Amy in US English. Choose a voice appropriate for the language you want spoken. Custom… lets you enter a known voice name or ID; it does not create or download a new voice by itself.
steps.checkpoint: Your selected voice appears in the field.

steps.title: Download another Piper voice
steps.narrationDraft: With Piper selected, use Download a voice…, choose a catalog entry, then click Download. Wait for Downloaded or Already installed. The successful download selects that voice. Click Save changes, then use read-aloud on a short reply to hear it.
steps.checkpoint: The new voice is available and speaks a short test.

steps.title: Choose when it speaks
steps.narrationDraft: Set Autonomous speech to On request only, Urgent / important, or Everything (natural pacing). These choices control spontaneous speech. They do not mean the microphone is always listening. An ongoing voice conversation has its own mute and exit controls.
steps.checkpoint: Genesis speaks only as often as you intended.

steps.title: Effects and the HAL choices
steps.narrationDraft: Voice effect → HAL 9000 changes the pitch, pace and room reverb of a local Piper or Windows voice. Set up HAL 9000 voice for me sets an effect and downloads the chosen local voice; save afterward. The separate HAL 9000 — real voice (clone, sidecar) engine needs its own running sidecar service. An effect is different from that separate engine.
steps.checkpoint: You know whether you selected an effect or a separate voice engine.

steps.title: If the chosen voice cannot speak
steps.narrationDraft: A missing configured Piper voice can use bundled Amy. Local speech can fall back to Windows and then browser speech when available. Check the voice status and test again. Genesis does not silently switch a local voice to a paid cloud service. An unavailable cloud or sidecar engine should be checked in its own configuration.
steps.checkpoint: You know how to get speech working again without enabling a cloud provider.

lessons.title: Use cloud listening or cloud voices
lessons.prerequisites: Internet and the matching provider’s API key or voice credentials.

steps.title: Listening and speaking can be mixed
steps.narrationDraft: You can listen locally and speak with a cloud voice, or use cloud listening and local speech. They are independent. Your main model can still be local. Choose each part in Settings → Voice & Vision and save. Cloud recognition sends audio to that provider; cloud speech sends the text to be spoken.
steps.checkpoint: You know which part, if any, will use a cloud service.

steps.title: For cloud recognition, choose OpenAI STT
steps.narrationDraft: Set Speech-to-text → OpenAI STT (cloud) and enter its key in STT API key. This field is separate from the main model’s key. Save and try a short recording. The Whisper size and device controls describe the local recognition route; they do not tune the cloud service.
steps.checkpoint: A small recording is recognised using the selected provider.

steps.title: For a cloud voice, choose its engine
steps.narrationDraft: Under Text-to-speech, choose OpenAI (cloud), ElevenLabs (cloud) or Azure (cloud). Enter the appropriate TTS API key and choose a voice supported by that engine, or use Custom for a known voice ID. This picture shows the OpenAI choice; select your own provider. Use the provider’s required configuration; an Azure credential or provider-specific voice identifier may need additional setup.
steps.checkpoint: The engine, credential and voice belong to the same provider.

steps.title: Save and test before a long conversation
steps.narrationDraft: Click Save changes. Play one short reply. Check connectivity, key access and the voice identifier if it fails. Provider charges and quotas are controlled by that company. Local voice never changes to cloud automatically: you explicitly choose the cloud engine and supply its key.
steps.checkpoint: You hear a short test in the voice you selected.

lessons.title: Have a conversation with the orb
lessons.prerequisites: The Modern interface, a connected model and working voice input/output.

steps.title: Open the circle beside Voice
steps.narrationDraft: In Modern, find Voice near the bottom of the left panel. Click its small circle for the orb conversation. Genesis opens a minimal screen and starts the voice session when ready. This is an ongoing conversation: your spoken turns go to the model without pressing Send for each one.
steps.checkpoint: The orb view opens and reports its voice state.

steps.title: Follow the words beneath the orb
steps.narrationDraft: The state tells you what is happening: Opening microphone, Listening, Waiting for your next words, Transcribing, Thinking, or Speaking. A brief pause can let it gather your next words before sending the turn. If it is thinking, give it a moment to work.
steps.checkpoint: You can tell whether it is listening or answering.

steps.title: Move the pointer to reveal controls
steps.narrationDraft: Move your mouse over the orb view to show controls. The microphone button mutes listening; the speaker button mutes sound. They are separate. Use the left chevrons to show the transcript and the right chevrons to show the browser panel. Panels can be resized.
steps.checkpoint: You can mute listening without losing the conversation.

steps.title: Interrupt when you want to speak
steps.narrationDraft: While it is thinking or speaking, tap the orb to interrupt the reply and speak. The microphone’s mute state still matters. Interrupting a voice reply is not the same as undoing an action or stopping every background task. Use the work controls for that.
steps.checkpoint: You know how to interrupt the spoken turn.

steps.title: Read along or watch browsing
steps.narrationDraft: Open Transcript to see the words and tool activity. Open Browser when Genesis uses its browser. Closing the browser panel hides the view; it does not mean all browser work has stopped. If a site needs you, follow the request and return control when ready.
steps.checkpoint: You can reveal the transcript while keeping the orb visible.

steps.title: End the session deliberately
steps.narrationDraft: Click the exit icon or press Escape to leave the focused orb conversation. End or mute the session when you do not want it listening. If audio recovery offers Retry audio, Save audio or Discard & reset, read that notice before choosing.
steps.checkpoint: You are back in the main interface and the voice session has ended.

lessons.title: Give a text-only model the ability to see
lessons.prerequisites: A working saved preset for a model that actually accepts images.

steps.title: The helper sees; your main model still answers
steps.narrationDraft: A language model that only reads text cannot see pixels. Genesis can ask a separate vision model to describe an image, then give that description to your main model. Think of one helper looking at a photograph and explaining it to another helper. This does not change the main model’s underlying abilities.
steps.checkpoint: You understand the two-model arrangement.

steps.title: Save the image model as a preset
steps.narrationDraft: First add and test the picture-capable model in Settings → Models. It may be local or cloud. Set Image input to Auto-detect, unless provider metadata is missing or wrong and you know the correct capability. Choosing “Vision / multimodal” does not make a text-only model capable of seeing.
steps.checkpoint: The secondary preset points to a real image-capable model.

steps.title: Choose the Secondary vision model
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Voice & Vision → Screen & desktop control. Under Secondary vision model, select that saved preset. It has its own provider, connection and model. A cloud helper can receive pictures even when your main language model runs locally; choose a local helper if you want that image processing local.
steps.checkpoint: The intended image model is selected.

steps.title: Choose how images are routed
steps.narrationDraft: Auto: primary → secondary fallback uses the resolved model if it can accept images, and the secondary when needed. Always use secondary preset sends every image through the selected helper. Disabled turns image-model routing off. The Legacy options exist for older dedicated configurations; a saved secondary preset is easier to manage.
steps.checkpoint: The selected routing choice matches what you want.

steps.title: Read the effective route, then try a picture
steps.narrationDraft: Click Save changes and check Effective route. A model may say it will be tested on first use until image input has been verified. Attach a simple picture and ask “Describe what you see.” Confirm the description is right before asking it to reason about a tiny label or complicated screen.
steps.checkpoint: The image is described correctly and the route status makes sense.

steps.title: Understand the limit of the handoff
steps.narrationDraft: Your text-only model reasons from the helper’s description, not from the original pixels. If the helper misses a detail, the main answer can miss it too. Ask for a specific region or a clearer screenshot. A local language model plus local vision helper keeps those model calls local; web tools and other cloud choices remain separate.
steps.checkpoint: You know why checking the image description matters.

steps.title: Screen reading has extra tools
steps.narrationDraft: OCR engine reads written text from a screen. Maximum Set-of-Marks targets limits numbered controls in a vision pass. These help screen tasks but do not replace permission to control an app. Computer use decides what Genesis may operate. The vision route is also used by image-file tools and Missions.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish reading the screen from permission to act on it.

lessons.title: Show Genesis the window you are using
lessons.prerequisites: Genesis desktop on Windows and another app window you want to show.

steps.title: Enable the screenshot shortcut
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Computer use → Appshots and turn on Enable Appshots. This desktop preference applies immediately. The status should say the shortcut is ready. You can also choose whether a sound plays after capture.
steps.checkpoint: The shortcut reports ready.

steps.title: Bring the other app to the front
steps.narrationDraft: Open the window you want to show Genesis. Press Left Alt + Right Alt together. Release both keys before taking another screenshot. Appshots captures the foreground app’s visible window and puts the image into your current conversation draft.
steps.checkpoint: The screenshot appears attached to the draft.

steps.title: Explain what you want and send
steps.narrationDraft: Return to Genesis. Check the screenshot, write something like “Explain this error message” or “Which button opens the settings?”, then press Send. The shortcut does not send the screenshot by itself. Your selected image route reads it after you send.
steps.checkpoint: The image and your question are sent together.

steps.title: Check before sharing
steps.narrationDraft: If the picture shows a private letter, key or personal information you did not intend to share, remove it from the draft. Choose a local vision route when you want picture interpretation to stay local. The screenshot only shows what was visible at capture time; it is not a live screen stream.
steps.checkpoint: You are sending exactly the window content you intended.

lessons.title: Follow and edit the working plan
lessons.prerequisites: A task with a working plan, or a request to make a plan.

steps.title: Ask for a clear plan
steps.narrationDraft: Try “Make a plan for organising these files. Show me the plan before making changes.” Genesis can use a live checklist for its current work. Plan opens it above the conversation; the right panel can also show an editable working plan.
steps.checkpoint: You can find the Plan control.

steps.title: Read the status marks
steps.narrationDraft: An empty mark means pending. A filled active mark means in progress. A check means done. The counter shows completed items out of all items. These are work-tracking labels; inspect the actual output before accepting that a job is finished.
steps.checkpoint: You know which step Genesis is currently working on.

steps.title: Edit the plan where it is editable
steps.narrationDraft: Click an editable task’s text to revise it. Use Add a step… to add an item. Status dots cycle the state; remove and reorder controls let you adjust the checklist. Edits to the live plan steer the active channel: Chat uses its chat plan, while Work and Autonomy use the feed plan.
steps.checkpoint: Your edited item appears in the plan.

steps.title: Use words when the goal changes
steps.narrationDraft: A checkbox does not explain why the task changed. Send a short message such as “Keep the originals; make copies instead.” If the change must happen before any further action, pause first. Collapse Plan when you want more room for the conversation.
steps.checkpoint: Both the plan and the message describe your updated goal.

lessons.title: Chat, Work, Autonomy—and your controls
lessons.prerequisites: A connected model. Use a small harmless task while learning.

steps.title: Find the three buttons at the top
steps.narrationDraft: In the Modern layout, the three small buttons at the top choose Chat, Work or Autonomy. The speech bubble means Chat, the briefcase means Work, and the orbit means Autonomy. Hover to read their names. The highlighted button tells you which mode is active. In Classic, the same choices have written labels.
steps.checkpoint: You can find all three mode buttons and recognise the selected one.

steps.title: Choose Chat for a request you want to guide
steps.narrationDraft: Chat is a conversation: you send a request, Genesis answers, then waits for your next message. It may use connected tools to fulfil that request, so Chat can do more than answer a question. Use it to explain a letter, rewrite a recipe, research a choice or work through a task together. Try: “Explain this letter in simple words, then wait for my questions.”
steps.checkpoint: You know Chat is useful when you want to steer one exchange at a time.

steps.title: Choose Work to carry out assigned jobs
steps.narrationDraft: Click the briefcase / Work button. A new Managed / Continuous switch appears beside the mode controls while Work is selected. Work looks for assigned work, including eligible projects and scheduled work; give the job a clear result and the files it needs. For example, create a project to organise your garden notes into a watering chart. The switch decides what happens after the assigned work runs out.
steps.checkpoint: You can select Work and see the extra two-choice switch.

steps.title: Managed finishes the assignments, then waits
steps.narrationDraft: With the switch on Managed, Genesis works through eligible assignments and waits when there is no assigned work to do. It does not need to keep inventing new projects to fill that idle time. Use Managed for a defined list of jobs: “Finish this invitation draft and put it in Review.” Check the actual result in the project or activity view. Managed is a good starting choice when you want a clear stopping boundary.
steps.checkpoint: You understand that Managed waits after assigned work is finished.
steps.tip: Managed can still use tools and take several steps. It does not mean one short chat reply, and it does not replace your review of the result.

steps.title: Continuous can find new useful work afterwards
steps.narrationDraft: Click the small switch to choose Continuous. It still gives assigned work priority. When those projects are in Review or Complete and there is no other eligible assignment, it can look for a new useful project to propose and prepare. Use this when you want ongoing assistance, such as exploring improvements to a hobby project. You are allowing activity beyond the original job, so inspect the plan, outputs and available tool permissions. Click the switch again to return to Managed.
steps.checkpoint: You can switch both ways and explain what Continuous adds.
steps.tip: Continuous does not mean publishing a result, spending money or approving it for you. Those actions still depend on their own authority and controls.

steps.title: Choose Autonomy for self-directed exploration
steps.narrationDraft: Click the orbit / Autonomy button when you want Genesis to choose and pursue its own activities within the tools and permissions you have given it. It can follow an interest, work on a project or reflect, rather than waiting for one chat message. This is more open-ended than an assigned Work queue. Its feed shows what it actually does. Mood, energy and rest indicators are software state, so judge the activity and results you can inspect.
steps.checkpoint: You understand that Autonomy can continue without a new message from you.
steps.tip: Use a limited, understandable set of tools on your first run. Pause when you want to read or redirect the activity.

steps.title: Choose the mode to match your intention
steps.narrationDraft: Use Chat for “Help me with this, and I will guide you.” Use Work → Managed for “Do these assigned jobs, then wait.” Use Work → Continuous for “Do my assigned jobs, then look for another useful project.” Use Autonomy for “Explore and choose your own activity.” For a large objective that needs an agreed contract, a dependency graph and separate verification, open Missions in the left panel. A Mission is its own process; it is not a fourth choice on the Work switch.
steps.checkpoint: You can choose a mode for a particular job, rather than treating them as three names for the same thing.

steps.title: Pause gives you time to read
steps.narrationDraft: Use Pause while Work or Autonomy is running when you want time to read or redirect it. The screenshot shows Work running, so its Pause control is visible. Read the resulting paused state. Pausing does not undo an action already taken.
steps.checkpoint: The work reports that it is paused and stays available to inspect.

steps.title: Resume the paused work
steps.narrationDraft: When you are ready, click Resume. This continues the paused loop. Send a clear correction first if the goal changed. Switching modes can cancel or redirect current companion work; pause first when you need to inspect an unfinished job, and read the confirmed state after changing mode.
steps.checkpoint: You know how to continue the paused job deliberately.

steps.title: Stop and Stop All have different effects
steps.narrationDraft: Stop ends current activity while keeping state for later. Stop All is the stronger companion reset and also resets its moods. In Modern these controls are compact icons; hover for the label. Mission pause and abort are separate controls inside the mission.
steps.checkpoint: You know which control to use for the activity you intend to end.

steps.title: The other compact controls
steps.narrationDraft: Consolidate asks Genesis to organise recent material into memory. Override is an explicit manual control for state constraints. You do not need either for ordinary chat. Check tool permissions in Settings rather than using an override as a routine shortcut.
steps.checkpoint: You can recognise these controls and leave them alone when you do not need them.

lessons.title: Organise a project on the board
lessons.prerequisites: A small project idea and a clear finished result.

steps.title: Open Projects
steps.narrationDraft: Click Projects. The columns are Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review and Complete. Backlog is for later ideas; To Do is ready work. Start with one small project, such as drafting a birthday invitation or organising a folder.
steps.checkpoint: You can see the project board.

steps.title: Create a clear project
steps.narrationDraft: Use the add control in the intended column. Give it a title and description. Say what the result should contain, where files should go and what Genesis should avoid. A project can contain smaller tasks and subprojects. Include facts it cannot guess.
steps.checkpoint: The project has a title, clear description and appropriate status.

steps.title: Choose the model and reasoning if needed
steps.narrationDraft: Project execution fields can select the model and reasoning for that work. Otherwise the companion configuration is used. A modest project can use a smaller local model; a hard project may need a more capable one. Keep the task narrow enough to check.
steps.checkpoint: You know which model the project is intended to use.

steps.title: Inspect Review before accepting
steps.narrationDraft: Work moves toward Review, where it waits for your decision. Open the result. Accept only after you have checked it; otherwise explain the needed revision. Complete means accepted work on the board, not an automatic promise that every generated fact is correct.
steps.checkpoint: You have inspected the actual output before accepting.

lessons.title: Set up a timed task
lessons.prerequisites: A task you want performed later, while Genesis is running.

steps.title: Open Schedule and add a task
steps.narrationDraft: Click Schedule in the left panel. Add a scheduled task using the page’s add control. Write the job in ordinary words, just as you would in chat. Include where the result should appear and what a successful result looks like.
steps.checkpoint: The task has a meaningful description.

steps.title: Check the time and repetition
steps.narrationDraft: Choose the scheduling options shown in the task editor. Read the resulting schedule carefully, including the local time. A repeating task should say what to do on each run. Avoid instructions that depend on an old date or a changing fact without telling Genesis to check it.
steps.checkpoint: The displayed schedule matches the time you intended.

steps.title: Choose the execution settings
steps.narrationDraft: For a duration task, choose Work to show Work model and Work reasoning. Autonomy tasks follow their mode configuration. Point events expose work settings when the action needs preparation. Check that any required files, provider key and tool connections are available. A cloud job needs internet; a local-only job can work offline if it has everything it needs.
steps.checkpoint: The task has access to its required model and material.

steps.title: Choose what a point event means
steps.narrationDraft: For one event at a particular time, select Point event. Deliver At prepares a result beforehand and holds it until the chosen time; give it a realistic preparation estimate. Start At begins work at that time. Notify At gives the scheduled notice. These are different promises, so choose the one you actually need.
steps.checkpoint: The action matches whether you want a result, a start or a notice.

steps.title: Check repeats, then create
steps.narrationDraft: Read Recurrence. Leave it on the once-only choice for a single event, or select the repeat pattern you intend. Re-read the title, instructions, time and action, then click Create. Cancel closes the editor without creating this new task. Start with a small test task before relying on a repeating job.
steps.checkpoint: The saved task appears in Schedule with the intended timing.

steps.title: Keep Genesis running and inspect the result
steps.narrationDraft: A local scheduler needs its running backend to execute work. A saved schedule does not mean a powered-off computer can run it. After a scheduled run, read the output and activity. Pause or disable the scheduled item when you no longer want repeats.
steps.checkpoint: You know when the task can run and where to check its output.

lessons.title: Give Genesis a bigger job
lessons.prerequisites: Mission Mode enabled and a clear objective with a result you can check.

steps.title: Use a mission when several pieces must fit together
steps.narrationDraft: Open Missions for a larger objective, such as comparing three weekend destinations with travel prices, lodging prices, a budget table and source links. These pieces depend on each other. A Mission agrees what success means, breaks the job into smaller tasks, checks their results and keeps the evidence. That structure is useful for a complicated report, a multi-part project or a software change. It still needs suitable models, tools and good instructions.
steps.checkpoint: You understand why a complicated job benefits from a Mission.
steps.tip: For a quick question, start with Chat. For a straightforward assigned project, Work may be enough.

steps.title: Answer the interview before it starts
steps.narrationDraft: Create a draft and answer the Mission Interviewer. Give it the missing facts: who is travelling, which dates, your starting point and the budget. Add useful files or references. Say what the result should contain and what it must avoid: “Compare only; do not book anything.” The interview turns a broad wish into a job Genesis can actually plan.
steps.checkpoint: The mission has the facts and boundaries needed for a contract.

steps.title: Choose the brains for the roles
steps.narrationDraft: In Settings → Missions → Role models, choose the mission default and any per-role models. Planner breaks the job down; Worker does one piece; Verifier checks that piece; CEO oversees the mission. These are roles, not necessarily four different installed models. One suitable model can fill several roles. Per-role backups are separate from the Chat/Work/Autonomy companion backup.
steps.checkpoint: You know who plans, works, checks and oversees the job.

steps.title: Agree on the result before signing
steps.narrationDraft: Read the proposed contract. Its acceptance conditions are the checks that define success: for example, “Compare three destinations; include travel and lodging costs and working source links.” Read the limits and allowed actions too. Edit a vague condition before signing. Signing starts planning for the agreed mission. The final decision that the delivery is acceptable remains yours.
steps.checkpoint: You have agreed on a result that you will be able to check.

steps.title: Genesis generates the task graph

anchor.label: Task graph · 5 live · 6 retained including retired

steps.narrationDraft: After signing, the Planner turns the contract into a task graph, often called a DAG. Think of a recipe with a sensible order: gather prices before adding up a budget; check the table before delivering it. Each task is one piece of work. Dependencies say which earlier pieces must be finished first. You do not have to draw the graph yourself. The dashboard fills it in as planning and further breakdown produce tasks.
steps.checkpoint: You understand where the task graph comes from and what it is for.
steps.tip: DAG means directed acyclic graph: work follows dependencies forward without a circular “A waits for B, B waits for A” loop. This interface presents it as an indented task list.

steps.title: Read the task states, not just the colours

anchor.label: Check lodging prices for the chosen dates

steps.narrationDraft: In Task graph, a task can be pending (not ready yet), ready (it can start), running, awaiting_verify (submitted for checking), or done (passed its check). An obsolete task is an older route replaced by replanning; it is retained as history. An indented row belongs to a larger phase. A task that is awaiting verification is not yet a checked result.
steps.checkpoint: You can tell a finished and checked task from work that is still waiting.

steps.title: Dependencies keep the job in a sensible order

anchor.label: Build the budget table from checked sources

steps.narrationDraft: In this example, the budget table needs both travel prices and lodging prices. If lodging is not checked yet, the table waits. Work in another ready branch can proceed when it is legally eligible. This does not mean several Workers act at once: Genesis performs Worker → Verifier → next Worker in sequence. The graph chooses the next useful piece and prevents later work from relying on unfinished prerequisites.
steps.checkpoint: You can explain why one task waits while another is eligible.
steps.tip: Try the small example below the screenshots. It demonstrates dependencies without running a real mission.

steps.title: The Worker produces; the Verifier checks

anchor.label: Check totals, links and the budget limit

steps.narrationDraft: The Worker uses the available tools to do a small assignment and submits its result and evidence, such as a document and source links. A fresh Verifier compares that work with the task’s checks and inspects the supplied evidence. If it passes, the task becomes done and dependent work can become ready. If it fails, the failure goes back into recovery. Verification helps catch mistakes; it cannot promise that every model judgment is correct.
steps.checkpoint: You understand why producing a file and verifying that file are different stages.

steps.title: A problem can lead to repair or a different route

anchor.label: Earlier search route (replaced after a blocked page)

steps.narrationDraft: Suppose a price source will not open, or the table totals are wrong. Genesis can retry a recoverable failure, ask for rework, examine why the attempt failed, split an oversized job into smaller pieces, or replan the affected branch. Strategic roles can suggest a better approach. Repeated failures are tracked so replacing a task does not erase its history. A provider outage or usage limit is handled as model trouble, with the configured role backup where applicable; it is not proof that your objective is impossible.
steps.checkpoint: You understand that recovery can change the approach while keeping the agreed goal.
steps.tip: It cannot invent missing access or guarantee a fix. The next step explains when it asks you.

steps.title: Choose how recoverable check-ins are handled
steps.narrationDraft: The running mission has Automatic mission recovery. Off means recoverable judgment check-ins can wait for you. On offers Let the CEO decide, then keep going or Always replan and keep going. Choose the behavior you intend, then use Save mission behavior. These choices help a long mission recover without asking you about every routine problem. They do not let it approve the final result, waive your conditions or grant itself new permissions.
steps.checkpoint: You can find the mission’s recovery controls and understand their limits.

steps.title: Some problems need something only you can provide

anchor.label: Tell Genesis which weekend you can travel

steps.narrationDraft: The Blocker inbox explains a missing fact, approval, credential or real-world action that needs you. Read the request, do only what you intend, and add a clear answer. In this example you supply the travel dates, then use Approve / Done. If you cannot help, choose Can’t and explain why. A mission may show WAITING_USER when it needs your judgment. Read the reason before resuming or changing the contract.
steps.checkpoint: You can recognise a genuine request for you and answer it deliberately.
steps.tip: Never mark a requested action done before doing it. Keep private credentials in their supported secure entry flow.

steps.title: Steer the mission without starting it over
steps.narrationDraft: Use Adapt plan to give the Planner a concrete correction, such as “Use train travel rather than flights.” Ask the council requests a strategic review. Use Edit contract when the actual goal, success conditions or authority need changing. A new plan can replace old task branches while retaining their history. Read the ledger and new tasks to see what was actually changed.
steps.checkpoint: You know the difference between adjusting the route and changing the agreed job.

steps.title: Pause or abort inside the mission
steps.narrationDraft: Use the mission’s Pause when you need time to inspect or redirect the job; resume it from the mission when ready. Use Abort to end that mission. These controls are separate from the three companion mode buttons and from Chat’s Stop controls. Read the resulting mission status after clicking. Pausing does not undo work already performed.
steps.checkpoint: You know which controls govern this mission.

steps.title: Progress and evidence make a long job easier to follow

anchor.label: Task graph · 5 live · 6 retained including retired

steps.narrationDraft: Genesis keeps the mission contract, task states, recorded evidence and event history. You can inspect the Task graph, acceptance progress and ledger instead of reconstructing the whole job from a long conversation. Eligible missions can recover saved progress after a restart, but unsaved thinking is not restored and a tool action may have happened before an interruption was recorded. This durable structure, small assignments and repeated checks are the reasons Missions suit complicated work.
steps.checkpoint: You know what the mission records and why that helps with a longer job.

steps.title: You decide whether the whole result is good enough
steps.narrationDraft: When the pieces are checked, Genesis performs final verification against the contract and reaches USER_SIGNOFF. Open the actual deliverables, read the sources and check each agreed condition. Accept only if the result meets them, or explain what needs more work. A series of completed tasks is progress; your final sign-off is the decision to accept the delivery. Automatic recovery cannot make that decision for you.
steps.checkpoint: You have checked the delivery and understand that final acceptance belongs to you.

lessons.title: Tune a mission to the job and model
lessons.prerequisites: Settings → Missions. A small mission you can inspect before a large one.

steps.title: Read recovery as a specific choice
steps.narrationDraft: Recoverable check-ins chooses whether a new mission asks you, deterministically retries/replans, or gives the CEO a bounded attempt and then continues. Automatic recovery cannot accept the final work for you, waive criteria, approve credentials or spend money. The running mission also has its own recovery controls.
steps.checkpoint: You know what recovery may continue and what still needs you.

steps.title: Give a weaker model smaller jobs
steps.narrationDraft: Worker leaf size limits the size of an individual worker assignment. Choose S when a smaller local model struggles with broad tasks. Larger phases can be broken down into smaller pieces. Worker execution floor controls the minimum step budget; it is separate from the estimated size.
steps.checkpoint: The job size suits your worker model.

steps.title: Choose models for the different roles
steps.narrationDraft: Planner divides the job; Worker does a piece; Verifier checks it; Council and Auditor offer strategic or independent review; Intake handles the interview; CEO oversees the mission. A contract can override Settings for that mission. Worker and Verifier run sequentially even when strategic reviews use concurrency.
steps.checkpoint: You can explain why the worker and verifier may use different models.

steps.title: Keep source reading large enough to be useful
steps.narrationDraft: The source limits control how much text is extracted, read per slice, or included directly. A large blueprint may need paging. A higher limit also consumes context. If an interview seems to miss a supplied document, inspect the reading activity and extracted material before assuming that simply increasing all limits will fix it.
steps.checkpoint: You know where document limits can affect the interview.

steps.title: A payment limit alone does not authorise purchases
steps.narrationDraft: A mission cost envelope records a planned limit. Real payment execution additionally needs the dedicated signed payment policy, an enabled payment path and a compatible verified connection. A no-funds test adapter cannot buy anything. Leave payment authority off unless you intend and understand that specific supported setup.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish a budget number from a payment permission.

lessons.title: Let Genesis use a browser
lessons.prerequisites: A supported browser. Browser Bridge setup for your own browser.

steps.title: Choose the browser route
steps.narrationDraft: Genesis has its own browser workspace with tabs and persistent Genesis sign-ins. To use your already-open personal browser, connect Browser Bridge. These are different routes. A browser inside Genesis does not automatically share every login from your personal browser.
steps.checkpoint: You know which browser route you want.

steps.title: Connect your own browser in Computer use
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Computer use → Control. Find your browser and use Set up when offered. Follow the extension setup for that exact browser. Connection status belongs to the browser where the extension is installed; setting up Chrome does not also connect Edge.
steps.checkpoint: The intended browser reports connected or paired.

steps.title: Understand the connection status
steps.narrationDraft: A browser that was paired but is closed may reconnect when opened. A disconnected browser is not necessarily missing its extension. Check the name and state before repeating setup. Any app, Genesis browser, Your browsers (Browser Bridge) and Documents & spreadsheets control different kinds of access.
steps.checkpoint: You can identify the connected browser and its allowed control.

steps.title: Ask for a simple browser task
steps.narrationDraft: Try a public page first: “Open this page and tell me its three main points.” You can watch the integrated browser using View → Browser. A site may block automation or require sign-in; a working connection does not guarantee access to every website.
steps.checkpoint: The correct page opens and the summary matches it.

steps.title: Take control for a request that needs you
steps.narrationDraft: If a site asks for sign-in, a code or CAPTCHA, use the request or browser handoff. Take control prevents Genesis from using that control surface while you act. Finish the required step yourself, then use Resume to return browser control. That does not automatically resume a paused mission or finished model turn.
steps.checkpoint: You understand the handoff and can return control deliberately.

steps.title: Leave advanced browser tuning until needed
steps.narrationDraft: In Voice & Vision, browser settings choose profile, channel, headless mode, the inside-Genesis panel and page timing. Headless hides the browser. Page-settle time lets a page finish loading; navigation gaps slow repeated visits. Choose visible browsing while learning so you can follow the actions.
steps.checkpoint: Your first browser task runs in a view you can observe.

lessons.title: Choose what Genesis may control
lessons.prerequisites: Settings → Computer use open.

steps.title: Start with the main control categories
steps.narrationDraft: The Control tab separates desktop control, the Genesis browser, your browsers, and documents. More apps adds services connected through MCP. Turning one on does not give every other category access. These permissions govern tools; a model request does not automatically override them.
steps.checkpoint: You can identify each category and its state.

steps.title: Allow the access your task needs
steps.narrationDraft: Enable the category needed for the task you intend, and check the per-browser or per-server entries. Computer use changes apply immediately. Browser Bridge and an MCP server must also be connected before their controls work.
steps.checkpoint: Only the intended task’s access is enabled.

steps.title: Use handoff while you act
steps.narrationDraft: When Genesis is controlling your desktop, the control bar can let you Take control. Use it before typing into the same surface. Once you finish, return control with Resume only if you want the automation to continue. Read its status after the handoff.
steps.checkpoint: You know how to avoid competing mouse and keyboard input.

steps.title: Read tools separately from permissions
steps.narrationDraft: In Settings → Plugins → Skills, individual tool switches can restrict available actions. A connected service, enabled tool and permitted computer category may all be needed for the same task. If an action is unavailable, check those layers rather than simply enabling everything.
steps.checkpoint: You know where to check an unavailable action.

lessons.title: Tools, plugins and connected apps
lessons.prerequisites: Settings → Plugins. Only install packages you trust.

steps.title: Skills are the actions Genesis can use
steps.narrationDraft: Open Plugins → Skills. Search for a tool to read its description and switch it on or off. A tool is an action; a skill can give instructions for using tools. Turning off an action can make a task unavailable. AI-created tools have their own controls.
steps.checkpoint: You can locate a tool and understand what it does.

steps.title: A plugin bundles capabilities
steps.narrationDraft: Open the Plugins tab. Use Add → Import a plugin for a local plugin folder. Importing lets you review the package. Read its capabilities and trust the specific reviewed version before turning it on. Plugins can contain code and instructions that run with Genesis’s access.
steps.checkpoint: You understand that importing and enabling are separate steps.

steps.title: Apps are connected services
steps.narrationDraft: The Apps tab holds service connections and their keys. Set up only the service your task needs, add its key where requested and turn on the connection. A key allows an API connection; it is not always the same as an interactive signed-in account. A connector may have only the capabilities its card describes.
steps.checkpoint: The service’s card shows its configured connection state.

steps.title: MCP connects an outside tool server
steps.narrationDraft: MCP servers is for a service that supplies tools through the Model Context Protocol. Its transport may be local stdio, Streamable HTTP or legacy SSE. Use the server’s documented command or URL, enable it and check that it connects. The server’s individual tools can also be restricted.
steps.checkpoint: You know where the server’s connection and tool list are shown.

steps.title: Hooks run at lifecycle events
steps.narrationDraft: Hooks can run reviewed commands at named events, such as before a tool action. They are an advanced option. A command can deny or modify an action according to its supported hook contract. Review the command and trust its version before enabling it. You do not need hooks for ordinary use.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish a hook from a chat tool or app connection.

steps.title: Use the quick page or full Settings
steps.narrationDraft: The left-panel Plugins page is a quick place to browse and switch capabilities. Manage opens fuller Settings controls for keys, imports and server editing. An OpenAI-compatible model endpoint does not automatically connect OpenAI account apps or every connector. Check the exact feature the integration offers.
steps.checkpoint: You know when to use the quick page and when to open Manage.

lessons.title: Let Genesis work on code safely
lessons.prerequisites: A code folder you own. Git available or the optional Git setup offered in Settings.

steps.title: Add the folder in Code
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Code → Overview. Add the code folder you want Genesis to work on. The page explains whether Git is ready. Git is the version tool used for snapshots and safe copies; if missing, Genesis can offer an optional private download with your consent.
steps.checkpoint: The intended code folder appears in the list.

steps.title: Use undo history
steps.narrationDraft: Open History. Snapshots record versions around Genesis’s edits. Take a snapshot now gives you a point you can return to. A snapshot is a saved code version, not a backup of all Genesis memories or your entire computer.
steps.checkpoint: You can see snapshots for the chosen code folder.

steps.title: Go back to an earlier version
steps.narrationDraft: Inspect Changes before choosing Go back here. Genesis takes a “Before going back” snapshot so that return is itself undoable. Select the correct folder and snapshot; unrelated files or data are outside the promise of a code snapshot.
steps.checkpoint: You know which saved version you are restoring.

steps.title: Try risky changes in a safe copy
steps.narrationDraft: Open Safe copies, choose the folder and name the experiment. Make a safe copy creates a separate working folder. Ask Genesis to work in that copy. The original stays available while you inspect the experiment’s result.
steps.checkpoint: The copy has a separate path you can give Genesis.

steps.title: Review before bringing changes back
steps.narrationDraft: Open the copy’s Changes or start a Code review. A review looks for likely problems; it is not proof that code works. Test the result. Bring back applies the copy’s changes to the original, with an undo point. Read any clash before choosing which version to keep.
steps.checkpoint: You have inspected and tested the changes before bringing them back.

steps.title: Keep local versions separate from online publication
steps.narrationDraft: Saving a code snapshot is local. Uploading code, creating a GitHub repository or opening a pull request makes an outward change and has separate controls. The next lesson walks through that connection.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish a local save from a GitHub upload.

lessons.title: Connect GitHub and share code
lessons.prerequisites: A GitHub account and a token with access appropriate to the repository.

steps.title: Connect in Code → GitHub
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Code → GitHub. Paste your GitHub token in the connection field and connect. A token is an access credential; keep it private and give it the access required for your intended repositories. Confirm the displayed account.
steps.checkpoint: The page shows the intended connected account.

steps.title: Download a repository or select a folder
steps.narrationDraft: The repository list can download a repository to a code folder. A repository is a project stored with version history. If you already have a local folder, add it under Code first. Confirm the download destination before editing.
steps.checkpoint: The intended repository or folder is available locally.

steps.title: Save local work before uploading
steps.narrationDraft: Inspect changed files and use the history/save controls to record a clear local change. A commit is a labelled saved version. A local save does not by itself upload code to GitHub. Include a short message explaining what changed.
steps.checkpoint: You can identify the local change you intend to upload.

steps.title: Choose the outward action deliberately
steps.narrationDraft: Put on GitHub creates an online repository from a folder; choose its name and privacy. Upload sends local committed changes to the configured remote.
